phases.title: Phase 0 · Foundations (sprint: Tue Nov 10 – Sat Nov 14, 8h/day)

chapters.title: Setup and Git
chapters.ref: Appendix A Installation, Appendix B Text Editors and IDEs (we use PyCharm instead of the book's VS Code), Appendix D Using Git
goals: Python and PyCharm installed; the project uses the .venv interpreter
Can open, hide and leave PyCharm's terminal with the keyboard (README → Working in PyCharm)
Shortcuts installed; `s` ends with "✓ In sync."
Can explain what a commit is and why we commit small and often

chapters.title: Getting Started
chapters.ref: Chapter 1 (use PyCharm where the book uses VS Code)
goals: Run hello_world.py from PyCharm's Run button and from PyCharm's terminal

chapters.title: Variables and Simple Data Types
goals: Use strings, numbers, f-strings and comments
Read a traceback and find the line that broke

chapters.title: Introducing Lists
goals: Add, remove, sort and index list items

chapters.title: Working with Lists
goals: Loop over a list
Write a list comprehension without looking it up (first declarative idea!)
Slice lists; know the difference between a list and a tuple

chapters.title: if Statements
goals: Write if/elif/else chains and boolean conditions

chapters.title: Dictionaries
goals: Store and loop over key/value data; nest lists and dicts

chapters.title: User Input and while Loops
goals: Use input(), while loops, break/continue and flags

chapters.title: Functions
goals: Explain return values vs side effects
Use positional, keyword, default and *args parameters
Split code into modules and import them

chapters.title: Classes
goals: Write a class with __init__ and methods
Use inheritance; know when not to

chapters.title: Files and Exceptions
goals: Read and write files with pathlib
Handle errors with try/except
Save and load data as JSON

chapters.title: Testing Your Code
goals: Write and run a pytest suite that passes
Use a fixture

chapters.title: Mini Project
chapters.ref: Saturday Nov 14: build ~6h, demo 1h, retro and Phase 1 planning 1h
goals: Student picks and scopes it (e.g. a command-line tracker that saves to JSON)
Has tests that pass
README explains how to run it
Demoed to mentor and signed off
Phase 1 project tracks chosen and first weekly goals written

chapters.title: Deployed App
goals: Web app is live at a public URL
README write-up: what it does, how it's built, what I'd do next
Work done on branches and merged through pull requests the mentor reviewed

phases.title: Phase 2 · Think in functions and declarative style (weeks 8–17)
phases.book: Composing Programs (John DeNero), composingprograms.com, plus CS 61A labs

chapters.title: Higher-Order Functions
goals: Pass functions as arguments and return them from functions
Write and explain a closure and a lambda

chapters.title: Hog
goals: All autograder tests pass locally
Mentor has reviewed one function I'm proud of and one I'm not

chapters.title: SQL Practice
chapters.ref: SQLBolt lessons, then the same queries in SQLite

chapters.title: Python for Data Analysis
chapters.ref: Addition, months 3–5, only for the data analyst route (role 2). Chapters 4–10, then a real dataset.
chapters.book: Python for Data Analysis, 3rd ed. (Wes McKinney), free online
goals: Load, clean, group and summarize a CSV or spreadsheet with pandas
Work in a Jupyter notebook
Done when: a notebook answers a real question about real data, with charts and a short written conclusion
Skipping the data route? `bin/learn skip add-pandas`

chapters.title: Declarative Refactor
goals: Rewrite one Phase 1 project with pure functions, comprehensions and generators instead of loops that change state
Tests still pass
Explain the before and after to the mentor

phases.title: Phase 3 · Write Python like an experienced developer (months 5–9)

chapters.title: Portfolio, Resume and Referrals
chapters.ref: Addition, from month 4 until the first developer job. One small task a week; runs alongside everything else.
chapters.book: No book: weekly tasks, plus a monthly mock interview with the mentor from month 7
goals: Every project README explains what it does, why, and how to run it
Resume puts projects first and education last
LinkedIn and GitHub profiles up to date
One meetup a month (log each one with `bin/learn note`)
Ask for referrals; log each application with `bin/learn note`
Monthly mock interview from month 7: one coding problem and one project walkthrough
Done when: hired as a developer

chapters.title: Grokking Algorithms and Practice Problems
chapters.ref: Addition, months 5–10, alongside Fluent Python. The book, plus 2–3 practice problems a week (LeetCode or similar), easy first, then medium.
goals: Use lists, hash maps, stacks, queues, trees and graphs, and know when each fits
Explain the Big-O of my own code
Done when: I can solve an easy problem in ~20 minutes and a medium one in ~45, explaining my thinking out loud
Log each practice problem with `bin/learn ex <site-id> "<name>"`

chapters.title: Linux, Docker and HTTP
chapters.ref: Addition, months 6–9, used in the capstone. The Linux Command Line, Docker's getting-started tutorial, MDN's HTTP overview.
chapters.book: The Linux Command Line (William Shotts), free online; Docker docs; MDN Web Docs
goals: Move around, search and read logs from the terminal without a file browser
Package an app with a Dockerfile and docker compose
Explain an HTTP request: method, URL, headers, status code, body
Done when: the capstone runs from one `docker compose up`, and I can debug a failing request with curl and the logs

chapters.title: Capstone
goals: Has a real user (ideally a tool for my job)
Type hints checked with mypy
Linting with ruff
Tests with pytest
Checks run on every push with GitHub Actions
Uses a database

phases.title: Phase 4 · Design and teamwork (months 9–18)
phases.book: Architecture Patterns with Python (Percival & Gregory), cosmicpython.com

chapters.title: TDD in High Gear and Low Gear
The Pragmatic Programmer
chapters.ref: One topic per week, discussed at the check-in
chapters.book: The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed. (Thomas & Hunt)
goals: Log one takeaway per topic in Remarks

chapters.title: Open Source Contributions
goals: 3 pull requests merged into real open-source projects (link each one here)
Reviewed at least 5 pull requests from the mentor or a peer
